name: Metoclopramide
drug_class: Dopamine D2 antagonist and 5-HT4 agonist (prokinetic antiemetic)
route_note: Oral tablets or solution, IV or IM injection, nasal spray; short-term use

discovery.by: Louis Justin-Besançon and Charles Laville (Laboratoires Delagrange)
discovery.note: Derived from procainamide during work on antiarrhythmic and local anaesthetic agents.

tagline: Dopamine-blocking prokinetic antiemetic limited by risk of tardive dyskinesia
summary: Metoclopramide is an antiemetic and prokinetic that blocks dopamine D2 receptors and stimulates 5-HT4 receptors. It is used for nausea and vomiting and diabetic gastroparesis, but long-term use is restricted because it can cause tardive dyskinesia.
mechanism: Blockade of D2 receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone reduces nausea and vomiting. In the gut, D2 blockade and 5-HT4 agonism enhance acetylcholine release from myenteric neurons, increasing oesophageal sphincter tone, gastric emptying and small-bowel transit.
At high doses it also blocks 5-HT3 receptors. Because it crosses the blood–brain barrier, it can cause extrapyramidal reactions and raise prolactin.
uses: Nausea and vomiting (including chemotherapy and postoperative)
Gastro-oesophageal reflux refractory to other therapy (US)
Facilitating small-bowel intubation and radiological examination

history.title: Discovery
history.detail: Metoclopramide is first described by Delagrange researchers in France.

history.title: Boxed warning
history.detail: FDA adds a boxed warning on tardive dyskinesia with long-term or high-dose use.

history.title: EU restrictions
history.detail: EMA restricts metoclopramide to short-term use (up to 5 days) at lower doses and removes several indications.

history.title: Nasal spray
history.detail: FDA approves Gimoti nasal spray for diabetic gastroparesis.

pk.metabolism: Hepatic: conjugation and N-dealkylation; CYP2D6 contributes

serious: Acute dystonic reactions, especially in young people
Methaemoglobinaemia in neonates and NADH-cytochrome b5 reductase deficiency
safety.boxed_warning: Tardive dyskinesia, often irreversible; avoid treatment longer than 12 weeks.

facts: Metoclopramide was developed from the antiarrhythmic procainamide.
CYP2D6 poor metabolisers need lower doses because exposure is higher.
